title: Mother believes son was surrendering when shot by police during south Edmonton bank robbery
article: The mother of a man who was shot by police while robbing a bank in south Edmonton in 2012 thinks her son may have been trying to surrender to the officers when he was killed.

Laura Grisch, who was testifying in a fatality inquiry on Wednesday, said her son may have been imitating a pose he had seen on television or in movies - holding the handgun limply above his head - as officers approached.

Mike Bronaugh, who was also known as Mike Grisch, was shot by police officers after he tried to rob a Canadian Western Bank in South Edmonton Common on Dec. 12, 2012. He died the next day in hospital.

Grisch said that she didn't think her son was trying to provoke the officers into shooting him and that it was a genuine attempt at a robbery where no one would get injured. Bronaugh had made an appointment at the bank and was there for nearly 20 minutes before the police arrived.

Bronaugh demanded a bank teller hand him 99 hundred-dollar bills and threatened to shoot someone if the cash was not produced in less than a minute. Police said Bronaugh brandished a gun after officers arrived on scene and refused to comply with their demands to drop it. Both officers then fired multiple shots at him.
Judge Laura K. Stevens said she wanted to hear Grisch testify to get an idea of the kind of person Bronaugh was.

Grisch said he was a boy who loved to read, in particular Stuart Little, which he once read twice in one evening. Grisch said he was kind and loving child who, at the age of two, tried to give away all his Halloween candy.
She said it was when he entered middle school that he started to get into trouble and he never completed Grade 10.
"He was always at his best when he was busy," said Grisch. His favourite job was working at a produce store when he was about 18 years old because it allowed him to work with people, she said.

In June 2010, Bronaugh was sentenced to six months in jail for possession of a dangerous weapon, carrying a concealed weapon and failing to comply with a court order. When he got out of jail he told his mother it had changed him for the better.
He had stopped smoking marijuana but, due to the conviction, he had trouble getting a job. He mentioned he was feeling depressed but didn't want to take anti-depressants.
"I think he was feeling defeated," Grisch said.
In August 2013, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team ruled the two officers were justified in fatally shooting the 24-year-old Bronaugh.
A report will follow the fatality inquiry, but no date has been set on when it will be completed.
